moduleTitle: SQE1 · Wills and Administration of Estates
title: Revocation of wills
subtitle: Destruction, later wills, and the effect of marriage, civil partnership and divorce
objectives: State the four recognised methods of revoking a will and the mental element each requires
Explain the automatic revocation of a will by marriage or civil partnership, and the narrow contemplation-of-marriage exception
Apply the divorce rule correctly, distinguishing lapse of a gift to a former spouse from revocation of the whole will

leadingAuthorities.role: The four methods of revocation: later will or codicil, writing declaring an intention to revoke, or destruction with intention
Automatic revocation of a will by marriage or civil partnership, subject to the contemplation-of-marriage exception
Effect of dissolution or annulment of a marriage: gifts and appointments to the former spouse lapse; the rest of the will survives
The equivalent revocation and dissolution rules for civil partnerships

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Students often treat revocation as a single idea — 'the will is cancelled' — when the SQE1 tests four distinct doctrines with four distinct triggers. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this note appears: 'You know the four methods — this lesson is about which one the facts are actually describing.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall of the revocation rules before. The test pool below leans towards fact patterns: expect scenarios where you have to identify which method of revocation (if any) has actually occurred.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and take your time over the four methods in s 20 — the rest of the lesson assumes you can list them without prompting before it moves to marriage and divorce.

overview.hook: A testator tears up her will in a fit of temper after an argument, then immediately regrets it and tries to piece it back together with tape. Is it revoked? The answer turns entirely on a single word most people never think to ask about: intention. This lesson is about the four doors out of a will — and the one door, marriage, that can close it without the testator lifting a finger.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 24 September 2026. The core revocation rules in the Wills Act 1837 are long-settled; the divorce/dissolution lapse rule under s 18A was itself the product of reform (1995) and remains stable law.

parts.heading: Four doors, one statute
parts.voice: structural — a reference-style part students will return to
body: Section 20 of the Wills Act 1837 gives four, and only four, ways a will can be revoked: (1) a later will or codicil that revokes it, expressly or by inconsistency; (2) a written document, executed like a will, declaring an intention to revoke; (3) destruction of the will by the testator, or by someone else in the testator's presence and at their direction; or (4) operation of law, principally on marriage or civil partnership.

The exam trap sits inside method (3). Destruction alone does nothing — the statute requires destruction 'with the intention of revoking' it. Burn the will by accident in a house fire, and it is not revoked; the contents can still be proved by other evidence, such as a copy or a solicitor's draft, if the court is satisfied the original existed and was not deliberately destroyed by the testator.

The other half of the trap is the reverse: partial or half-hearted destruction. Tearing a will into pieces with the settled intention to destroy it revokes it even if you never manage to burn every fragment. But a symbolic scratch, or crossing out the signature alone without more, may not be enough — the act must be one the statute recognises as destroying the document, done with the necessary intention at the same time.

components.definition: The intention to revoke — the mental element that must coincide with the physical act of destruction (or with the written declaration) for revocation to be effective. Destruction without this intention, or intention without any act, revokes nothing.

interaction.prompt: Name the four methods of revoking a will under s 20 of the Wills Act 1837.
acceptableAnswers: later will or codicil, written declaration, destruction with intention, operation of law
a later will, a writing declaring intention to revoke, destruction with intention, and marriage/civil partnership
interaction.modelAnswer: A later will or codicil; a document executed like a will declaring an intention to revoke; destruction by the testator (or by another in their presence and at their direction) with the intention to revoke; and operation of law, chiefly automatic revocation by marriage or civil partnership.

parts.heading: Destruction: the statute's exact words
parts.voice: argumentative — states the rule precisely, then tests its edges
body: Section 20 does not say 'destroying the will revokes it'. It requires destruction 'by the testator, or by some person in his presence and by his direction, with the intention of revoking the same'. Every word here does work an examiner can test.

'By the testator' — a stranger who destroys the will without the testator's direction, even believing they are doing the testator a favour, does not revoke it; that will may still be proved by other evidence if its contents can be reconstructed.

'In his presence and by his direction' — a solicitor who burns a client's will over the telephone, on instructions but out of the client's sight, has not satisfied the statute. The testator must be physically present when someone else does the destroying.
'With the intention of revoking' — this is why accidental loss, accidental destruction, or destruction while a testator lacks the mental capacity to form the intention, does not revoke a will at all.

components.text: No will or codicil, or any part thereof, shall be revoked otherwise than ... by the burning, tearing, or otherwise destroying the same by the testator, or by some person in his presence and by his direction, with the intention of revoking the same.
elements: An act of burning, tearing, or otherwise destroying the document
Done by the testator, or by another person in the testator's presence and at their direction
Done with the intention of revoking the will

interaction.prompt: A testator's will is accidentally destroyed in a house fire while the testator is asleep upstairs. Applying s 20, is the will revoked?
options: No — there is no intention to revoke, which s 20 requires alongside the act of destruction
Yes — any destruction of the physical document is enough
Yes, but only if the testator later confirms they are glad it burned
interaction.explanation: Section 20 requires destruction with the intention of revoking. Accidental destruction, however total, satisfies the physical limb but not the mental one, so the will is not revoked — its contents may still be proved by secondary evidence such as a copy.

parts.heading: Marriage revokes the will you already made
parts.voice: case-narrative — walks through the rule's practical bite before naming the exception
body: Section 18 imposes a rule many clients never expect: getting married automatically revokes any earlier will, in full, by operation of law — no tearing, no burning, no written declaration required. A meticulous will made at 25 is worthless the moment its maker marries at 40, unless a fresh will is made after the wedding.

The policy reason is straightforward: marriage fundamentally changes a person's financial and family obligations, and the law assumes a will made before that change no longer reflects the testator's likely wishes. The same rule applies to civil partnership under s 18B.

There is one narrow, precisely worded exception. A will (or a specific gift within it) survives marriage if it was made 'in expectation of' the marriage to a particular, named person, and is expressed to be conditional on that marriage taking place. A will made shortly before a wedding, referring only to marrying 'my fiancé' in general terms, or made in expectation of marrying someone unspecified, will not qualify — the exception is read narrowly, and the intended spouse must be identified.

components.label: The contemplation-of-marriage exception, in three requirements
points: The will (or the relevant gift) must show it was made in expectation of marriage
The marriage must be to a specific, identified person — not marriage in general
The will must be expressed to be conditional on that marriage taking place

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact that stops this will from being automatically revoked by the wedding.
interaction.scenarioText: Priya makes a will in March expressly stating it is made in contemplation of her forthcoming marriage to Tom, and that it is to take effect only if that marriage takes place. She marries Tom in June.
tappableSpans: expressly stating it is made in contemplation of her forthcoming marriage to Tom
that it is to take effect only if that marriage takes place
interaction.correctSpan: expressly stating it is made in contemplation of her forthcoming marriage to Tom
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the operative wording. Naming Tom specifically, and framing the will as made because of and conditional on marrying him, is exactly what s 18's exception demands — a generic reference to 'my forthcoming marriage' would not be enough.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the clause identifying a named, specific person as the intended spouse — that is what distinguishes a will that survives marriage from an ordinary will that s 18 automatically revokes.

parts.heading: Divorce does not revoke — it edits
parts.voice: direct — sets up the trap the tests will probe
body: This is the rule most commonly confused with s 18, and examiners know it. Divorce or dissolution of a civil partnership does NOT revoke the will. It leaves the will standing and simply edits it: under s 18A, any gift to the former spouse, and any appointment of the former spouse as executor or trustee, takes effect as if the former spouse had died on the date the decree absolute (or dissolution order) was made.

Everything else in the will remains fully effective. If the will named a substitute beneficiary in case the spouse predeceased, that substitute now takes. If it did not, the gift falls into residue (or, if it was the residuary gift itself, the estate may pass on a partial intestacy) — but the rest of the will, and any gifts to other people, are untouched.

The trigger is decree absolute or the dissolution order — not separation, and not simply filing for divorce. A will made during a marriage that later separates but never formally divorces is not affected by s 18A at all; the former spouse (still legally the spouse) can still inherit.

components.title: Marriage vs divorce: two different effects on a will
components.description: Contrasts the whole-will revocation on marriage with the narrower lapse-only effect on divorce.

nodes.label: Whole earlier will revoked, unless the contemplation-of-marriage exception applies
Will remains valid; only gifts/appointments to the former spouse lapse, as if they had died on the date of dissolution

components.textAlternative: Marriage revokes an existing will in full unless a narrow exception applies. Divorce, by contrast, does not revoke the will at all — it only removes gifts and appointments made to the former spouse, treating them as though they had predeceased the testator on the date of dissolution.

interaction.prompt: Put these events in the order needed to trigger the s 18A lapse rule for a specific gift to a former spouse.
items: Testator makes a will leaving the residue to their spouse
Testator and spouse later divorce, and decree absolute is granted
The gift to the former spouse is treated as if they died on the date of decree absolute
The residue passes as though the will contained no gift to them (e.g. to any substitute beneficiary, or on partial intestacy)
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct — the will has to exist and name the spouse first; the lapse only bites once decree absolute is actually granted, and only then does the substitution or partial intestacy analysis follow.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the sequence again: nothing happens to the gift until decree absolute is granted — separation or filing for divorce is not enough, and the consequence (substitute gift or partial intestacy) only follows after the lapse takes effect.

parts.heading: Applying it: which door, if any, was used
parts.voice: Socratic — poses a compound scenario before resolving it
body: In application questions, the facts will rarely tell you which section is in play. You are expected to work backwards from what happened to the document, or to the testator's marital status, and identify the correct doctrine — including the possibility that nothing has been revoked at all.

A useful discipline: first ask whether a physical act was done to the document (destruction, or a later document) — that is s 20 territory, and you must check for the coinciding intention. If nothing was done to the document itself, ask whether the testator's marital status changed — that is s 18 or s 18A territory, and you must check whether it was a new marriage (whole will revoked, subject to the exception) or a divorce (only the former spouse's gifts lapse).

Students lose marks by reaching for the more dramatic answer — 'the will is revoked' — when the facts actually describe a narrower lapse, or no effect at all. Precision about which rule, and how far it reaches, is what separates a pass-standard answer from a fail here.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often say that divorce 'revokes the will', by analogy with marriage, and then apply the marriage rule (whole-will revocation) to a divorce scenario.
components.whyItsWrong: Divorce triggers s 18A, not s 18. The will survives; only the former spouse's gifts and appointments lapse. Confusing the two sections leads students to wrongly conclude that a divorced testator has died intestate when in fact most of the will remains fully effective.

interaction.prompt: A testator's will leaves £50,000 to her husband and appoints him sole executor, with the residue to her sister. The couple later divorce, and decree absolute is granted. What is the effect on the will?
options: The whole will is revoked and the estate passes on full intestacy
The £50,000 gift and the executor appointment lapse; the residuary gift to the sister remains fully effective
Nothing changes — divorce has no effect on a will made during the marriage
The former husband still takes the £50,000 but loses only the executorship
interaction.explanation: Section 18A applies: on decree absolute, gifts and appointments to the former spouse are treated as if he had died on that date. The £50,000 gift and the executorship both lapse, but the will is not revoked — the residuary gift to the sister, untouched by s 18A, remains fully effective.

testPool.prompt: A testator's earlier will contains no clause revoking prior wills, but a later, validly executed will covers the whole estate on inconsistent terms. Is the earlier will revoked?
options: Yes — a later will can revoke an earlier one by inconsistency, without an express revocation clause
No — only an express revocation clause can revoke a prior will
No — the two wills must be read together and reconciled
Yes, but only the inconsistent clauses are revoked, never the whole document
testPool.explanation: Section 20 permits revocation by a later will or codicil, and this can occur by necessary inconsistency between the two documents, not only by an express revocation clause.

testPool.prompt: Which of the following, without more, is NOT a method of revocation recognised by s 20 of the Wills Act 1837?
options: A later will revoking the earlier one by inconsistency
A signed and witnessed document declaring an intention to revoke
Verbally telling a solicitor, in a phone call, that the will should be treated as cancelled
Tearing up the will with the intention of destroying it
testPool.trapExplanation: An oral instruction, however clear, is not one of the recognised methods. A declaration of intention to revoke must itself be in writing and executed with the same formalities as a will (s 20); a phone call, however sincerely meant, achieves nothing on its own.
testPool.explanation: Section 20 is exhaustive: a later will, a formally executed written declaration, or destruction with intention. Oral statements of intention are not a recognised method.

testPool.prompt: A testator, in a rage, tears his will into four pieces intending to destroy it, then immediately regrets it and sticks the pieces back together with tape so the whole document is legible again. Is the will validly revoked?
options: No — because the pieces were later reassembled, the destruction is treated as if it never happened
Yes — the tearing, done with the intention to revoke, is effective the moment it occurs; taping it back together afterwards does not undo the revocation
Yes, but only if a witness saw the tearing take place
No — a will can only be revoked by destroying it completely beyond any possibility of reconstruction
testPool.explanation: Revocation by destruction takes effect at the moment of the act done with the requisite intention. A change of heart afterwards, however immediate, does not revive the will — the testator would need to execute a fresh will or a valid codicil to reinstate its terms.

testPool.prompt: Under s 20, destruction by a person other than the testator can revoke a will. What must be true of that other person's conduct for revocation to be effective?
options: It must occur in the testator's presence and at the testator's direction
It is effective provided the testator later ratifies it in writing
It is effective provided the testator is a beneficiary under the will
It is effective if the person reasonably believed the testator wanted the will destroyed
testPool.explanation: Section 20 permits destruction 'by some person in his presence and by his direction'. Destruction by a third party out of the testator's presence, or without a clear direction from the testator, does not satisfy the statute, however well-intentioned.

testPool.prompt: A testator marries, having made no will beforehand mentioning the marriage. She had made a will five years earlier leaving everything to a former partner. What happens to that earlier will on marriage?
options: It is automatically revoked in full by operation of s 18
It remains valid but the former partner's gift lapses
It becomes valid only for gifts to blood relatives
Nothing — marriage has no automatic effect on an existing will
testPool.explanation: Section 18 automatically revokes an existing will on marriage or civil partnership, in full, unless the narrow contemplation-of-marriage exception applies. Nothing here suggests the will was made in expectation of this specific marriage.

testPool.prompt: A testator makes a will stating: 'This will is made in expectation of my marriage.' She marries eight months later. Does the will survive the marriage under the s 18 exception?
options: Yes — any reference to an expected marriage is sufficient
No — the exception requires the will to identify a specific, named intended spouse and be conditional on marrying them, which this generic wording does not do
Yes, provided the marriage occurs within twelve months of the will
No — the exception was abolished and marriage always revokes a prior will
testPool.trapExplanation: Students often assume any mention of an upcoming marriage is enough to trigger the exception. It is not — the exception is construed narrowly and requires the will to name the specific intended spouse and be expressed as conditional on marrying that person; generic wording like this fails.
testPool.explanation: The s 18 exception is narrow: it requires the will to be made in contemplation of marriage to an identified person and expressed to be conditional on that marriage. Generic language referring to 'my marriage' without naming anyone does not qualify, so the will is revoked.

testPool.prompt: A testator's will states it is made 'in contemplation of my marriage to James Okafor' and is 'conditional on that marriage taking place'. The couple marry as planned. What is the status of the will?
options: Revoked — all wills are revoked by marriage regardless of their wording
Unaffected by the marriage — the s 18 exception is satisfied
Valid only as to gifts made to James, all other gifts lapse
Void from the outset, because a will cannot be made conditional on a future event
testPool.explanation: The will identifies a specific intended spouse and is expressed to be conditional on marrying that person, satisfying the s 18 exception in full. The will is unaffected by the marriage and remains fully valid.

testPool.prompt: A married testator's will leaves his entire estate to his wife and separately leaves his classic car to his brother. The couple divorce and decree absolute is granted, but the testator never updates the will before dying. What happens to the residuary gift to the former wife?
options: It lapses, as if the former wife had died on the date of decree absolute
It remains valid because the will was never revoked
It is automatically redirected to the brother in addition to the car
It is reduced by half but the former wife still takes something
testPool.explanation: Section 18A treats a gift to a former spouse as if they had died on the date of decree absolute. The residuary gift to the former wife lapses; because there is no substitute gift of residue, this triggers a partial intestacy as to the residue, while the specific gift of the car to the brother is unaffected.

testPool.prompt: Which statement best captures the difference between the effect of marriage and the effect of divorce on an existing will?
options: Both revoke the will in full — divorce simply does it retrospectively from the date of the marriage
Marriage revokes the whole will (subject to a narrow exception); divorce leaves the will standing and only causes gifts and appointments to the former spouse to lapse
Marriage has no automatic effect; only divorce automatically alters a will
Marriage and divorce both only affect the appointment of an executor, never substantive gifts
testPool.trapExplanation: The most common error is treating divorce as a mirror image of marriage — assuming it also revokes the whole will. It does not: s 18A operates far more narrowly, editing out only the former spouse's gifts and appointments.
testPool.explanation: Marriage triggers whole-will revocation under s 18, subject to the contemplation-of-marriage exception. Divorce triggers the narrower s 18A lapse rule, leaving the rest of the will, and any gifts to other beneficiaries, fully effective.

testPool.prompt: Which event triggers the s 18A lapse rule for gifts to a former spouse?
options: The date the couple physically separate
The date one party first files a divorce petition
The date decree absolute (or the dissolution order) is granted
The date the couple sign a separation agreement
testPool.explanation: Section 18A is triggered by decree absolute (for marriage) or the dissolution order (for civil partnership) — formal legal ending of the relationship, not mere separation or the start of divorce proceedings.

testPool.prompt: A testator and his wife separate and live apart for three years, intending never to reconcile, but never formally divorce. The testator dies, and his unrevoked will leaves everything to 'my wife'. What is the effect of the long separation on that gift?
options: The gift lapses because the marriage has broken down in substance
The gift is unaffected — s 18A requires decree absolute or a dissolution order, and mere separation, however long, does not trigger it
The gift is reduced to reflect the length of the separation
The will is automatically revoked by the separation
testPool.explanation: Section 18A only bites on formal dissolution or annulment. However long a couple has lived apart, if they remain legally married, a gift to 'my wife' remains fully effective — a stark illustration of why keeping a will updated matters.

testPool.prompt: Do sections 18B and 18C of the Wills Act 1837 apply the same revocation and dissolution rules to civil partnerships as ss 18 and 18A apply to marriage?
options: Yes — civil partnership is revoked by entering the partnership, and dissolution operates the same lapse-only rule as divorce
No — civil partnerships are entirely outside the Wills Act scheme
No — civil partnership dissolution revokes the whole will, unlike divorce
Yes for revocation, but dissolution has no effect on gifts to a former civil partner
testPool.explanation: Sections 18B and 18C mirror ss 18 and 18A for civil partnerships: entering a civil partnership automatically revokes an earlier will (subject to an equivalent contemplation exception), and dissolution causes gifts and appointments to the former civil partner to lapse rather than revoking the whole will.

testPool.prompt: A testator's will appoints her husband as sole executor and leaves her residue to him, with no substitute named. After decree absolute is granted, the testator dies without making a new will. Who administers the estate and who benefits from the residue?
options: The former husband remains executor and takes the residue, because s 18A does not affect appointments, only gifts

The former husband's appointment as executor lapses and the residuary gift lapses, so administration follows the rules for an estate without a named executor and the residue passes on a partial intestacy
The will is void and the whole estate is administered on full intestacy
The former husband keeps the executorship but the residue passes to the Crown
testPool.trapExplanation: A common error is assuming s 18A only touches beneficial gifts and leaves executor appointments untouched. It expressly covers both: any appointment of the former spouse as executor or trustee also lapses, exactly like a beneficial gift.
testPool.explanation: Section 18A applies to appointments as well as gifts. Both the executorship and the residuary gift to the former husband lapse as if he had died on the date of decree absolute; without a substitute named, the residue passes on a partial intestacy, and an administrator (rather than the named executor) will need to be appointed.

testPool.prompt: A will contains a specific gift to the testator's cousin, plus a residuary gift to the testator's wife. The couple later divorce with decree absolute granted, and the testator dies without altering the will. Which parts of the will are affected by s 18A?
options: Only the gift to the wife; the gift to the cousin is entirely unaffected
Both gifts equally, since divorce revokes the will as a whole
Neither gift, because s 18A only applies to appointments of executors, not beneficial gifts
Only the gift to the cousin, because s 18A protects gifts to spouses specifically
testPool.explanation: Section 18A only affects provisions made to or in favour of the former spouse. The gift to the cousin, an entirely separate beneficiary, is untouched; only the residuary gift to the wife lapses under the lapse rule.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The single most common mistake in this lesson's test items is treating divorce as a mirror image of marriage and assuming it revokes the whole will. It does not — s 18A only strips out gifts and appointments to the former spouse, leaving the rest of the will intact.
